# Pronouncing Asanga: a guide for the curious

Saying **Asanga** aloud is harder than reading it on ​a screen, and more rewarding. The restored spelling is a compressed pronunciation guide: every accent and macron is an instruction. This post unpacks those instructions — the reconstructed sound, the phoneme-by-phoneme record, ‌the kindred forms in neighboring languages — and then zooms out to the full record around the name: its Devanagari writing, its mythology, its cult, and its modern life as a Unicode domain. ‌Whether you arrive as a linguist, a reader of myth, or a domainer, you will leave able to say the name the way the evidence suggests it was said — and able to ​type it the way it was written.

## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Asanga
- **ASCII form:** asanga
- **Meaning:** "Without attachment"
- **Domain of influence:** Yogacara, Mind-Only
- **Pantheon:** Buddhist
- **Restoration:** ASCII-equivalent form
- **Original script:** असन्ग ​(Devanagari)

## Overview

**Asanga** (*asanga*) — Yogacara, Mind-Only · Without attachment — belongs to the Buddhist tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Yogacara, Mind-Only". The name means "Without attachment".

**Asanga** is yogacara, ​mind-only. The name means "Without attachment" and belongs to the buddhist tradition.

PuniCodex restores the name as **Asanga** and serves its temple at [its temple](https://punicodex.com/asanga/). The restoration needs no distinctive letters or diacritics ​its ASCII form would lose. The plain ASCII form *asanga* survives as a modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends ​as philologically complete.

The name is attested in Devanagari as **असन्ग**. Etymologically it means "Without attachment".

The ASCII form *asanga* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; ‌it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. Phoneme by phoneme:

For the modern speaker, the closest ‌approximation is: Say "asanga" with the stress and length implied by the scholarly restoration "Asanga".

The ASCII form "asanga" is a DNS compromise; the restoration "Asanga" preserves the name's scholarly dignity.

The pronunciation ​given above reconstructs the sound world in which Asanga was invoked. Modern speakers should not expect exact identity with ancient phonology; the reconstruction is a scholarly compass, not a performance prescription. The ‌restoration Asanga keeps the prosodic information visible even when the name is typed in plain ASCII.

## Mythology

The stories of Asanga place yogacara, mind-only at the center of a living mythological world.

### Origins ​(Myth)

Asanga appears in buddhist tradition as yogacara, mind-only. The name's meaning, "Without attachment", shapes the narratives told about this figure.

### Worship and Memory (Cult)

Devotees and later tradition-keepers preserved Asanga in ritual, ​text, and iconography, ensuring the name survived into the modern scholarly record.

The myths of Asanga survive in fragments, summaries, and later retellings. Each version reflects the interests of its tellers — ​poets, priests, philosophers, and scholars. The PuniCodex entry does not privilege a single version; it gathers the attestations so that readers can compare them. The restoration Asanga gives the figure a stable name ​around which these variants orbit.

### Two Brothers, One Teaching (The Brothers)

Asanga and his younger half-brother **Vasubandhu** — arguably the two most consequential Buddhist philosophers after Nāgārjuna — were born, the story runs ​(Xuanzang preserves it in his *Great Tang Records of the Western Regions*), to a brahmin of Kauśika lineage; their mother, the legend adds, resolved that one son should master the Mahāyāna and ‌the other its rival, the analytical Abhidharma of Kaśmīr. Vasubandhu became the encyclopedist of the *Abhidharmakośa*; Asanga wandered and meditated until he founded **Yogācāra**. Then the elder brother executed the gentlest ambush in ​the history of ideas: feigning a mortal illness, he had disciples read him a Mahāyāna sūtra and plant objections that only the Mahāyāna could answer — until the great critic recanted on ‌the spot and joined the school he had spent his career refuting. Vasubandhu's conversion doubled the school's firepower: the *Viṃśikā* and *Trimśikā* became its core. The myth explains a real fact: **half of ​the Indian Mahāyāna was written by one family** — brotherly love as the engine of a philosophical revolution.

### Twelve Years, a Wounded Dog, and Maitreya (The Vision)

The founding vision of Yogācāra is ‌a story about **compassion first**. Asanga, the tradition says (Xuanzang; the Tibetan historians Bu ston and Tāranātha repeat it), spent **twelve years** in solitary retreat awaiting a vision of the future Buddha ​**Maitreya** — and saw nothing. Despairing on his way down the mountain, he met a dog dying in the road, its open wounds alive with maggots; to save both creature and worms he ‌cut flesh from his own thigh and reached to lift the maggots with his tongue. The dog vanished: it was **Maitreya**. The bodhisattva then carried Asanga bodily to **Tuṣita heaven**, where he received ​the five great treatises — *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*, *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*, *Madhyāntavibhāga*, *Dharmadharmatāvibhāga*, *Ratnagotravibhāga*. Modern scholarship — Frauwallner most forcefully — argues Asanga wrote them himself. The interpretive point survives either way: a philosophy of mind ‌founded by a man whose breakthrough came through the **gut** — the dying dog was the last rung of the ladder.

### Yogācāra, the Practice of Mind-Only (The School)

What Asanga built — with ​Vasubandhu and their lineage — the tradition called **Yogācāra**, "practice of yoga," and its opponents called *cittamātra*, "mind-only." Its masterworks, the *Mahāyāna-saṃgraha* ("Compendium of the Mahāyāna") and the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, set out a psychology ​of awakening: the **store-consciousness** (*ālayavijñāna*), a deep repository in which the seeds of deeds and habits sleep, waiting to sprout as the world; the **three natures** — the imagined (the snake), the ‌dependent (the rope), the perfected (the seeing); and the radical claim that the "external world" is a construction of consciousness, no more independent than a dream is independent of the dreamer. The *Saṃdhinirmocana ‌Sūtra* supplied the school's scriptural charter, with its doctrine of the three turnings of the wheel. The interpretive meaning: suffering was re-described from metaphysics into **psychology** — and liberation as a rewiring ‌of perception, perception seen at last as the whole stage.

## Symbols & Iconography

The iconography associated with Asanga concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:

- ​**Name** — The restored form Asanga, carrying scholarly and cultural weight.
- **Domain** — Yogacara, Mind-Only

Symbols function as a visual shorthand: they allow devotees and artists to recognize Asanga across media and centuries. ​The attributes listed above are not decorative; each one encodes a claim about power, identity, or function. The restored spelling Asanga carries the same precision in textual form.

- **The wounded dog** — ‌The dying dog whose maggots he moved with his tongue — the act of compassion that revealed Maitreya, and the founding parable of Yogācāra: insight comes through the heart, not the head
- **Maitreya's ​tower** — Tuṣita heaven, where the five treatises were received — Yogācāra's scriptural charter is literally from the future
- **The mirror** — The school's favorite image in later East Asian art — perception ​like a mirror: images arise, none stick; Asanga's name, 'without attachment,' is the mirror wiped clean
- **The storehouse (ālaya)** — The ālayavijñāna, the warehouse consciousness where seeds of karma sleep and sprout ‌— his school's most influential and most argued concept
- **The three natures** — Imagined, dependent, perfected — Asanga's map of how the mind builds its world and how it sees through the building

## ​Archaeology & Evidence

No monument, inscription, or artifact in the current PuniCodex corpus is yet assigned to Asanga with certainty. That absence should be read honestly: for a Buddhist name of this type ​the material record is expected to be thin, and the primary evidence remains the textual testimony gathered in the Scholarly Sources section.

Were such evidence to surface, it would take recognizable forms: ‌votive or dedicatory inscriptions naming असन्ग, sanctuary or cult remains tied to yogacara and iconography matching its traditional attributes (name and domain). Each candidate would be weighed against the reconstructed form of the ​name before entering the scholarly record.

## Realm & Domain

**Asanga** is yogacara, mind-only. The name means "Without attachment" and belongs to the buddhist tradition.

### Sacred Name

The restoration Asanga returns the figure ‌to scholarly recognition.

### Yogacara

Central domain: yogacara, mind-only.

### Living Tradition

Honored in buddhist myth, cult, and cultural memory.

### Unicode Restoration

Preserved as a flagship temple despite the unregistrable plain-ASCII form.

### Yogācāra

The 'practice ​of yoga' school — Abhidharma rewritten as psychology: suffering located in the structure of consciousness itself.

### The Vision of Maitreya

Twelve years of retreat, a dying dog, and transport to Tuṣita heaven — ​where the future Buddha dictated the five great treatises.

### The Two Brothers

He and his half-brother Vasubandhu wrote half the Indian Mahāyāna — the gentle ambush that converted the greatest critic of ​the Mahāyāna.

## Across Cultures

Within the Buddhist tradition, closely related names in the corpus include [[akshobhya|Akṣobhya]], [[amitabha|Amitābha]], [[amoghasiddhi|Amoghasiddhi]], [[arhat|Arhat]], [[avalokiteshvara|Avalokiteśvara]], and [[bhaisajyaguru|Bhaiṣajyaguru]].

Cross-cultural identifications are rarely one-to-one. Asanga may be likened to figures ​in neighboring traditions without being identical to them. The PuniCodex crosslink index records these resonances as relationships, not equations. The restored form Asanga makes such comparisons possible across language boundaries.

## Cultural Legacy

Asanga ‌remains a touchstone for understanding buddhist religion, art, and identity.

The modern afterlife of Asanga includes scholarly editions, artistic adaptations, and popular references. Each reuse renegotiates the figure’s meaning for a new ‌audience. The PuniCodex temple participates in that afterlife by ensuring that the restored name Asanga remains findable and citable.

## A ​Meditation

To contemplate Asanga is to hold the idea of yogacara, Mind-Only in the mind and to ask what of it endures. The name means "Without attachment" — and a name that carries ​its meaning so openly invites meditation rather than mere recollection. The tradition remembers the name as yogacara, Mind-Only · Without attachment.

Sit with the restored form — Asanga — and the diacritics ‌themselves become the practice: each mark is a small act of attention, a refusal to let the plain ASCII form *asanga* stand in for the whole. What the tradition preserved in this name, ‌the restoration asks the reader to preserve in turn.

## A Closer Look at the Marks

A restored name is a small ‌map. In the case of **Asanga**, the map does not lead through diacritics or special letters, because the source tradition wrote the name in Devanagari rather than in the Latin alphabet. The ASCII ​form *asanga* and the restored form share the same letters; the restoration is a decision about which conventional spelling should serve as the public reference.

That decision is not cosmetic. The original script ‌attestation carries semantic and phonetic information that no romanization can fully reproduce. By fixing one conventional spelling as the canonical domain form, the project prevents the drift that happens when a name ​is romanized differently in every article, map, and database. The breakdown still lists each character — **a**, **s**, **a**, **n**, **g**, **a** — so visitors can see exactly what is being carried forward ‌and what is not. What looks like "no change" is, in fact, a deliberate choice to keep the name stable, searchable, and addressable.

## Asanga in Its Tradition

**Asanga** does not stand alone. ​It belongs to the Buddhist tradition, where it is counted among 26 names in the PuniCodex lexicon. Its sphere — Yogacara, Mind-Only — places it beside other figures who govern similar aspects of ‌experience. The restored spelling is therefore not only a philological decision; it is a way of keeping the name in the company of its kin. When the address bar shows **Asanga**, it marks ‌the boundary between a generic search term and a named entry in a living catalog of myth. That catalog is the point of the project. Every restored name is a vote for ​specificity: the web should know the difference between a figure and a keyword, between a tradition and a trend. **Asanga** is one such vote.
